policy.official: A league or club publication. Only these may ground a row in the verified master list (data/archive.json).
policy.partner: A free, keyless, publicly reachable hosted feed (ESPN's site endpoints). Useful for live game state, timestamps and leads. Never grounds a verified archive row on its own.
policy.unofficial: Public social or aggregator material (Mastodon, Google News RSS, CBS-style trackers, X/Instagram/Facebook/TikTok/Reddit). Leads and context only: never auto-published as a verified claim.
policy.rule: A lane may only ever be shown with its tier label. An unofficial or partner item is never presented as a verified in-game injury. Absence of a report never implies a player is healthy.
policy.organisation: Every lane is labelled with its tier (official / partner / unofficial), its category, the latency class a reader should expect, the timestamp precision it actually carries, and how it can be reached (keyless JSON, HTML, link-out or blocked). A lane that cannot be reached is listed as blocked rather than dropped.

sources.name: Club head-coach press-conference transcript
sources.what: A verbatim club transcript of the coach's postgame or midweek availability, including reporter questions about specific injuries.
sources.proves: The coach's own words about a player being evaluated or day-to-day, e.g. Hafley on Caleb Douglas's ankle: 'I think it's too early to tell.'
sources.latency: Same day or the morning after the availability.

verification.method: Fetched in full this session and read line by line while testing the Dolphins' Week 2 candidates.

sources.notes: Often confirms that an injury exists without saying it happened in the game, so it is a follow-up lane, not an in-game lane. Douglas therefore stays a lead, not a row.

sources.name: NFL Player Health & Safety (league medical hub)
sources.what: The league's own health-and-safety hub: concussion data, medical-officer briefings, equipment and emergency-care programmes.
sources.proves: What the league itself says about concussion protocol, emergency action plans and season-long injury data.
sources.latency: Season-level; published in reports and features.

verification.method: Fetched and read this pass; the page is the league's medical hub (player care, equipment, resources).

sources.notes: Context only. It documents the protocol a blue tent or a concussion evaluation refers to; it never reports a specific in-game event.

sources.name: NFL.com scoreboard
sources.what: The league's own scoreboard page: which games are live, the clock and the score.
sources.proves: Game state and kickoff times, from the league itself.
sources.latency: Seconds on the page; not a machine feed.

verification.method: Fetched NFL.com/scores: it listed Thursday Night Football Falcons at Packers for Sep 24, 8:15 PM ET, and the full Week 3 slate with 2026 records.

sources.notes: Reader-facing fallback when the partner header lane is blocked. A scoreboard never proves an injury.

sources.name: Club newsroom index (all 32 clubs, machine-read)
sources.what: Each club's own news index, read automatically by scripts/clubscan.py so in-game sentences can be found without a human opening 32 sites.
sources.proves: Which club articles exist, when they were published and what they say verbatim — including in-game sentences.
sources.latency: Minutes to hours after the article is posted.

verification.method: The index pattern is read for all 32 clubs by the discovery scan; the host list is checked against the ledger's official allowlist by a test, and each club's probe result is stored in data/clubscan-state.json (blocked clubs are recorded, never skipped).

sources.notes: Two-read stability promotion: a sentence may only enter the ledger after the identical text is read twice, the sentence names the club, and the article's date resolves to a real game.

sources.name: ESPN core play-by-play (plays with wall-clock times)
sources.what: Every play of a game as JSON, each with its down, distance, clock and — the part that matters here — a wall-clock timestamp to the second.
sources.proves: When a play happened in real time, to the second, and what the play said. It does not prove an injury unless the play text itself says so.
sources.latency: Seconds after the play; the feed is a partner API, not a league statement.

verification.method: Fetched this pass: the CIN@HOU game returned 207 plays with per-play wallclock stamps (kickoff 2026-09-20T17:02:38Z) and per-play participant references.

sources.notes: The closest a free feed gets to 'when did this happen'. scripts/watch_live.py polls it during games and logs any play whose own text carries an availability phrase.

sources.name: ESPN game summary injuries section
sources.what: The per-game summary payload, which can carry an injuries section with a player, a status and a provider note.
sources.proves: A partner feed's own status line for a player in that game, dated to the minute.
sources.latency: Minutes; updated during and after a game.

verification.method: Endpoint confirmed reachable and CSP-allowed; the reader walks the JSON for any injuries array and drops records without an athlete or status, so an unknown shape yields nothing rather than a guess.

sources.notes: Partner tier: shown as PARTNER FEED · UNVERIFIED and never allowed to ground a verified row.

sources.name: TheSportsDB NFL events (free, keyless)
sources.what: A free keyless schedule/results API used to enumerate a day's NFL games and their venues.
sources.proves: Which games were played on a date, the venue and the final score. Never an injury.
sources.latency: Updated after games.

verification.method: Fetched this pass for 2026-09-20: three games returned with timestamps, venues, scores and a YouTube highlight link each (e.g. ATL 3-34 CAR).

sources.notes: Second independent schedule lane: if ESPN game enumeration fails, this one can still date a club sentence.

sources.name: Pro Football Talk (NBC Sports) injury news
sources.what: A reporter-staffed newsroom that posts in-game developments within minutes, with a published clock time.
sources.proves: What reporters say happened, attributed to insiders, with a publication timestamp.
sources.latency: Minutes after the play; often the first public wording for a cart or a tent.

verification.method: Article text read this pass: 'Jaxson Dart questionable to return with knee injury', published Sept 21, 2026 08:39 PM, describing the medical tent and the locker room visit.

sources.notes: Leads only: it can never ground a verified row, and anything it reports stays labelled UNOFFICIAL.

sources.name: RotoWire NFL player news
sources.what: A live player-news wire that cites reporters and timestamps every note.
sources.proves: What another outlet reported, with its own attribution chain.
sources.latency: Minutes.

verification.method: Listed in this pass with dated notes (e.g. Brooks surgery Sept 23; Dowdle day-to-day Sept 22).

sources.notes: Aggregator: useful for noticing a report early, never evidence.

sources.name: RotoWire NFL injury report
sources.what: A weekly injury-report page that mirrors designations and adds reporter sourcing.
sources.proves: Designations as another outlet read them; a cross-check on the league's own report.
sources.latency: Daily through the practice week.

verification.method: Listed this pass; the Week 2 edition was found during the Bengals@Texans grounding search.

sources.notes: Practice designations only. Never grounds an in-game row.

sources.name: FantasyPros NFL injury news
sources.what: A player-news aggregator with timestamps and original-outlet attribution.
sources.proves: Where a report first appeared, and how several outlets worded it.
sources.latency: Minutes.

verification.method: Lane listed this pass from the project's own aggregator set; the page was not opened line by line, so it is recorded as existence-only.

sources.notes: Only ever a discovery hint. Nothing from an aggregator enters the ledger.

sources.name: Cincinnati Enquirer live game blog
sources.what: A newspaper's live game blog, updated during play with clock-stamped entries.
sources.proves: What a beat writer saw during the game, to the minute.
sources.latency: Seconds to minutes while a reporter types.

verification.method: Read this pass in search results: entries carry times like '2:03 pm ET September 20, 2026'.

sources.notes: A human reader can watch a club's beat blog while the page is open. Automated reading is not attempted.

sources.name: Saints Wire live blog (USA TODAY network)
sources.what: A team-site live blog with clock-stamped entries, including in-game injury observations.
sources.proves: What its reporter saw (e.g. Christian Mahogany leaving with a non-contact injury) with a timestamp.
sources.latency: Minutes.

verification.method: Read this pass: the Week 1 entry describes Mahogany's non-contact exit and Ben Bartch replacing him.

sources.notes: Its Mahogany note is the lead for the one-row Detroit-New Orleans game, and it is not evidence: a club sentence is still required.

sources.name: Sports Illustrated team pages
sources.what: Team-scoped news indexes that republish club injury-report tables and reporter notes.
sources.proves: A second reading of a club's own injury-report table, plus beat commentary.
sources.latency: Hours.

verification.method: Index read this pass ('Texans Injury Report Lists Nico Collins Among 4 Players Out vs. Bengals').

sources.notes: Discovery lane for finding which club page to read; the club page itself is the source of record.

sources.name: NFL on YouTube (official league channel)
sources.what: The league's own video channel: highlights and sideline clips that can show an event after the fact.
sources.proves: What a clip shows — a cart, a tent, a player walking off — when a human watches it.
sources.latency: Minutes to hours after the play.

verification.method: Listed as a human-followed link. No keyless read tier exists for video, so nothing is scraped.

sources.notes: Treated as unofficial here: a clip is an observation a person makes, not a league statement the page can quote.

sources.name: Reddit NFL search (link-out)
sources.what: A human-readable search over r/nfl, where fans post sideline observations within seconds.
sources.proves: What fans say they saw, at best. Frequently wrong about which player it was.
sources.latency: Seconds for a human; the JSON tier is blocked (403) for automation.

verification.method: The JSON tier was re-probed and refused (403), so the lane is offered only as a link a reader can open.

sources.notes: The one-click links on the live rail use this lane. Fan posts never enter the ledger or the log as evidence.

sources.name: TikTok search (link-out)
sources.what: Short-form video search: sideline clips sometimes surface here before a newsroom writes anything.
sources.proves: Only what a person watching the clip decides it shows.
sources.latency: Seconds for a human reading it.

verification.method: Link-out lane: no keyless read tier, so it is never fetched by the page or by CI.

sources.notes: Grouped with Instagram and Facebook, which the page already offers as one-click searches.

sources.name: NFL.com game pages (Game Center)
sources.what: One page per game: kickoff time and venue, the week's injury status table for both clubs, team stats and highlights.
sources.proves: Game context and the league's own published status table. It is not a live injury feed and cannot ground an in-game row.
sources.latency: status table refreshed with each official injury report; otherwise as fast as the game clock

verification.method: Opened the Week 3 Falcons at Packers game page: it shows the 8:15 PM kickoff at Lambeau Field and the injury tables naming Ebukam (hamstring, out), Bako-Bewele (knee, out), Banks (toe, out) and Reed (neck, out).

sources.notes: Useful when a reader wants the league's own page for a game rather than a provider's. Statuses on it are pregame declarations, so they belong in context and follow-ups, never in an in-game row.

sources.name: 'The NFL Report' injury segments
sources.what: Short post-game video segments, each titled with the player and the reported injury (for example, a season-ending patellar tendon tear, or a quarterback in concussion protocol).
sources.proves: A league-published summary of an injury after the game, and sometimes the later outlook. The page's own text is only a sentence, so quote exactly that.
sources.latency: minutes to hours after the game; not an in-game feed

verification.method: Opened the Week 2 notable-injuries segment and its sibling clips: each clip names the player and the injury in the page title and description.

sources.notes: Good for a dated follow-up claim on an existing row. A video title is not a second source: if only a clip says something, label it as league-published commentary, not club confirmation.

sources.name: nflverse open data
sources.what: Community-run release archive of play-by-play, rosters and box scores for past and current seasons, downloadable as CSV/parquet.
sources.proves: A second, independent, free record of what happened play by play after the fact. It carries quarter and game clock, not wall-clock timestamps, and it is not an official source.
sources.latency: hours to a day after games; not usable for in-game alerts

verification.method: Opened the repository: an active public project (141 commits, release workflow updated within the last week) publishing automated NFL data.

sources.notes: Kept as the clearest free play-by-play alternative to the ESPN core API, for verification and season-long context. Unofficial tier: it can never ground a verified row.

sources.name: Pro-Football-Reference
sources.what: Independent statistics reference: per-player game logs, box scores, snap counts and season history.
sources.proves: Whether a player appears in a game log and what the box score recorded. It is a reference, not a reporting outlet, and it is not official.
sources.latency: updated after games; often not until the following day

verification.method: Fetched the site home page; it served the current 2026 player index. Individual player and game pages were not opened line by line this session, so the lane is recorded as a reference only.

sources.notes: Use it to sanity-check that a player was actually in a game before a claim is published, never as the evidence for one. Scraping is rate-limited by the site's own robots policy: prefer one-off manual checks.
